provenance: Level 2 was authored fresh in the learner-first curriculum overhaul on 2026-11-09 (see docs/planning/korean-curriculum-overhaul-2026-11-09.md). A further pass added one gap grammar point (formal noun copula N입니다/입니까?) and a teaching guide for every point (prisma/seed-data/teaching-guides/), applied by teachLesson() at the lesson boundary. Lesson 22 (reported speech) is labelled an optional bridge — it sits near or beyond the usual TOPIK I beginner boundary. -(으)ㄹ지라도 and written nominalization -(으)ㅁ were deliberately omitted as higher-level material. Not independently reviewed by a Korean educator; treat as a curated draft, not vetted teaching content.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ까요?
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ까요? to ask for a suggestion or offer to decide together: 'Shall we...?' or 'Should I...?'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take the verb stem. Use 을까요 after most consonant-ending stems and ㄹ까요 after vowel-ending stems: 가다 → 갈까요?

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 같이 갈까요? — Shall we go together? 같이 갈까요? asks 'Shall we go together?' It invites the listener into the decision.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is not just an ordinary future question. 갈 거예요? asks about a plan; 갈까요? asks for a suggestion or opinion.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Shall we go together?
What movie shall we watch?

cards.englishHint: Shall we leave now?
Shall I open the door?
Shall we eat lunch now?

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ래요
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ래요 to express what YOU would like to do or ask what the listener would like to do.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take the action stem. Add 을래요 after most consonant stems or ㄹ래요 after vowel stems: 마시다 → 마실래요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 차를 마실래요. — I will have tea. 저는 차를 마실래요 says 'I'd like to have tea', expressing a personal choice.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: A speaker's preference differs from a fixed future plan. Don't use this form to assert another person's wishes as if you could know them.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I will have tea.
What do you want to do this weekend?

cards.englishHint: I will have water.
Do you want to buy this?
I want to rest at home.

grammarPoints.title: -겠- (speaker's intention)
grammarPoints.hint: The ending -겠- can express the speaker's determination or intention, as in a formal announcement that they will take responsibility for an action.
grammarPoints.description: The ending -겠- can express the speaker's determination or intention, as in a formal announcement that they will take responsibility for an action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Insert 겠 after the verb stem and before a sentence ending: 하다 → 하겠습니다, 노력하다 → 노력하겠어요. The exact degree of resolve depends on context.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 제가 먼저 하겠습니다. — I'll do it first. 제가 먼저 하겠습니다 uses 겠 to express the speaker's intention to go first rather than a factual prediction.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Compare -(으)ㄹ게요 for a listener-oriented commitment and -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a future plan. The same 겠 also has a distinct guessing use.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I'll do it first.
I will contact you again.

cards.englishHint: I'll take responsibility.
I'll make a real effort.
I'll come again tomorrow.

grammarPoints.title: -겠- (guess / inference)
grammarPoints.hint: The same -겠- ending can express what the speaker infers about a present or future situation.
grammarPoints.description: The same -겠- ending can express what the speaker infers about a present or future situation. It can soften an empathetic comment or suggest something seems likely.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Insert 겠 after a verb or descriptive stem, then add the appropriate ending: 춥다 → 춥겠어요; 맛있다 → 맛있겠어요. Read the surrounding context to tell a guess from an intention.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 많이 피곤하시겠어요. — You must be very tired. 많이 피곤하시겠어요 expresses the speaker's impression that the other person must be very tired.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't treat every 겠 as 'will'. In 맛있겠어요 the speaker is evaluating how food seems, not announcing an intention to be delicious.

lessonExamples.englishHint: You must be very tired.
This food looks delicious.

cards.englishHint: It must be cold outside.
That must be good news.
That must be really difficult.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)려고 하다
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)려고 하다 to say you intend or plan to do something.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 으려고 after most consonant stems, 려고 after vowel stems, and then 해요: 공부하다 → 공부하려고 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 한국어를 공부하려고 해요. — I plan to study Korean tomorrow. 내일 한국어를 공부하려고 해요: the speaker intends to study Korean tomorrow.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Planning to do something is different from doing it now. Don't treat -려고 하다 as the ongoing-action marker -고 있다.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I plan to study Korean tomorrow.
I plan to meet a friend this weekend.

cards.englishHint: I'm planning to buy groceries today.
I plan to read a book tonight.
I plan to go to Korea next year.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)러 가다
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)러 가다/오다 to say you go or come somewhere for a PURPOSE: 'go to eat', 'come to study'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 으러 after most consonant stems or 러 after vowel stems, then 가요/와요: 먹다 → 먹으러 가요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 밥을 먹으러 가요. — I am going to eat. 밥을 먹으러 가요 means going somewhere in order to eat a meal.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This pattern goes with movement verbs such as 가다 or 오다. It does not work as a general connector for every action.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I am going to eat.
I am going to meet a friend.

cards.englishHint: I'm going to get coffee.
I went to buy a book.
I am going swimming.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㅂ시다
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㅂ시다 for 'Let's...', a suggestion to do something together in formal polite speech.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a vowel-ending stem add ㅂ시다; after most consonant stems add 읍시다: 가다 → 갑시다, 먹다 → 먹읍시다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 이제 갑시다. — Let us go now. 이제 갑시다 means 'Let's go now', including the speaker in the proposed action.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: It is more formal or forceful than -(으)ㄹ까요?; it may sound too direct in relaxed conversation.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Let us go now.
Let us eat lunch together.

cards.englishHint: Let's study together.
Let us meet again tomorrow.
Let us rest here for a moment.

grammarPoints.title: -ㅂ니다/-습니다
grammarPoints.description: Use -ㅂ니다/-습니다 for a FORMAL statement about an action or description, such as an announcement.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Drop 다 from the verb or adjective. Add ㅂ니다 after a vowel stem or 습니다 after most consonant stems: 가다 → 갑니다, 먹다 → 먹습니다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 매일 한국어를 공부합니다. — I study Korean every day. 저는 매일 한국어를 공부합니다: 공부하 + ㅂ니다 → 공부합니다, expressing a regular action formally.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Noun identity needs the copula 입니다, not an action-verb stem ending pasted onto a noun. ㄹ-final stems also lose ㄹ before ㅂ니다.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I study Korean every day.
The bus will arrive soon.

cards.englishHint: I work for a company.
The weather is nice today.
I do not have time now.

grammarPoints.title: -ㅂ니까/-습니까?
grammarPoints.description: Use -ㅂ니까/-습니까? for a FORMAL question about an action or description.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Drop 다, then add ㅂ니까 after a vowel stem or 습니까 after most consonant stems: 가다 → 갑니까?

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 지금 어디에 갑니까? — Where are you going now? 지금 어디에 갑니까? is a formal way to ask 'Where are you going now?'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Noun questions use N입니까? ('Are you a student?'). Do not try to turn a noun into a verb by adding -ㅂ니까.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Where are you going now?
Do you study Korean?

cards.englishHint: Where do you live?
Is this book good?
Do you have time?

grammarPoints.title: -ㄴ다/-는다 (plain statements)
grammarPoints.hint: Plain Korean is used in diaries, essays, narrative descriptions and some close informal speech.
grammarPoints.description: Plain Korean is used in diaries, essays, narrative descriptions and some close informal speech. It states an action without marking politeness toward the listener.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For present action verbs, attach ㄴ다 after a vowel stem and 는다 after a consonant stem: 가다 → 간다, 먹다 → 먹는다. Descriptive verbs often keep the dictionary-like form: 좋다.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 나는 지금 책을 읽는다. — I read a book now. 지금 책을 읽는다 uses 읽는다 to narrate the ongoing action in plain style, not to address someone politely.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not assume every plain statement is a direct social equivalent of 해요. Plain style is often used in writing; adjectives and nouns follow different rules.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I read a book now.
He goes to school every day.

cards.englishHint: My younger sibling eats rice.
A friend is coming tomorrow.
A bird flies in the sky.

grammarPoints.title: N입니다 / N입니까?
grammarPoints.description: Use 입니다 for 'is/am/are' with a NOUN in formal polite speech, and 입니까? for a question.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 입니다 or 입니까? directly to the noun: 학생 + 입니다 = 학생입니다; 학생 + 입니까? = 학생입니까?

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 학생입니다. — I am a student. 저는 학생입니다 is 'I am a student' in formal speech, compared with 저는 학생이에요 in everyday polite speech.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse 입니다 (noun identification) with -ㅂ니다/-습니다 (an action or descriptive verb's formal ending).

notes.title: Copula, not verb stem
notes.content: 학생 + 입니다 → 학생입니다. For a verb, use the separate formal ending, e.g. 갑니다.

notes.title: Register
notes.content: This register is common in speeches, formal introductions, announcements and some customer-facing situations.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I am a student.
Is that person a teacher?

cards.englishHint: I am a doctor.
Is this a book?
This place is a hospital.

grammarPoints.title: Special honorific verbs: 계시다 / 드시다 / 주무시다
grammarPoints.hint: Some frequent actions have special respectful verbs instead of just adding -(으)시- to the ordinary verb.
grammarPoints.description: Some frequent actions have special respectful verbs instead of just adding -(으)시- to the ordinary verb. Which form you use depends on who performs the action.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + Special honorific verbs: 계시다 / 드시다 / 주무시다

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 계시다 for the location of a respected person (있다 → 계세요), 드시다 for their eating or drinking (먹다/마시다 → 드세요), and 주무시다 for sleeping (자다 → 주무세요).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 할머니께서 집에 계세요. — Grandmother is at home. 할머니께서 집에 계세요 uses 계세요 to describe the respected grandmother's presence at home.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not use these forms for yourself to show politeness. Honorifying the subject is not the same as speaking politely to the listener.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Grandmother is at home.
Is Father eating? (respectfully)

cards.englishHint: The teacher drinks tea.
Grandfather is sleeping.
Mother is at home.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어도 되다
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어도 되다 to ask for or give permission: 'May I...?' or 'It's okay to...'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: First make the action's 아/어 form: 앉다 → 앉아. Then add 도 돼요: 앉아도 돼요, literally saying that sitting is okay.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 여기 앉아도 돼요? — May I sit here? 여기 앉아도 돼요? asks whether sitting here is allowed. 앉아도 is the possible action; 돼요? asks whether it is acceptable.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 돼요 is the correct spelling of 되어요 here, not 되요. Compare permission with obligation -아/어야 해요.

lessonExamples.englishHint: May I sit here?
You may take pictures.

cards.englishHint: May I drink water here?
You may go now.
May I read this book?

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 주다 (do for someone)
grammarPoints.hint: Use -아/어 주다 when someone does an action for another person's benefit.
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어 주다 when someone does an action for another person's benefit. It highlights who receives the favor rather than simply whether the action happened.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + -아/어 주다 (do for someone)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use the action verb's 아/어 form, then a separate 주다: 도와주다 ('help') lexicalized; 읽다 → 읽어 주다, 써 주다. The recipient may take 에게 or 한테.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구에게 편지를 써 줬어요. — I wrote a letter for a friend. 친구에게 편지를 써 줬어요 means the letter-writing was done for the friend's benefit, not just that the letter exists.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -아/어 주세요 is the request form already in Level 1; this point covers ordinary statements about helping actions, including past tense.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I wrote a letter for a friend.
I read a book to my younger sibling.

cards.englishHint: The child opened the door for me.
A friend took a photo for me.
Mom chose clothes for me.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)면 안 되다
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)면 안 되다 to say an action is NOT allowed: 'must not' or 'shouldn't'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 으면 or 면 to the verb stem, then 안 돼요: 늦다 → 늦으면 안 돼요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 여기에서 담배를 피우면 안 돼요. — You must not smoke here. 여기에서 담배를 피우면 안 돼요: 피우다 → 피우면 names the condition 'if you smoke'. 안 돼요 marks that action as not allowed.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is stronger than not wanting to do it (안). Don't confuse 'must not' with 'don't have to'.

lessonExamples.englishHint: You must not smoke here.
You must not be late for class.

cards.englishHint: You must not take pictures here.
You must not enter here.
You must not use your phone during class.

grammarPoints.title: -지 마세요
grammarPoints.description: Use -지 마세요 to politely tell someone NOT to do an action: 'Please don't...'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Start with the action stem: 뛰다 → 뛰. Attach 지 마세요 to tell the other person politely not to do it: 뛰지 마세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 여기에서 뛰지 마세요. — Please do not run here. 여기에서 뛰지 마세요 directly asks the listener not to run here.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't use 안 + -세요 as the usual prohibition. -지 마세요 targets the listener; -(으)면 안 돼요 expresses a rule or prohibition.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Please do not run here.
Please do not worry.

cards.englishHint: Please don't leave now.
Please do not eat too much.
Please do not open the door now.

grammarPoints.title: -기
grammarPoints.description: -기 turns an action into a noun-like activity: 'reading', 'studying', or 'doing'. That lets you say you like or dislike an action.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 기 to a verb stem. Then add the particle the surrounding sentence needs: 읽기 + 를 = 읽기를.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 책 읽기를 좋아해요. — I like reading books. 저는 책 읽기를 좋아해요: 책 읽기 ('reading books') becomes the thing that the speaker likes.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The noun-like -기 is not the whole polite sentence ending. To say 'before doing', add 전에 after -기: 먹기 전에.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I like reading books.
Getting up early is difficult.

cards.englishHint: I like cooking.
I like walking every day.
Learning Korean is fun.

grammarPoints.title: -고 나서
grammarPoints.description: Use -고 나서 to make it clear that one action FINISHES before another begins.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 고 나서 to the first action stem, then state the next action: 먹다 → 먹고 나서.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 밥을 먹고 나서 커피를 마셔요. — After eating, I drink coffee. 밥을 먹고 나서 커피를 마셔요: 먹다 becomes 먹고 나서, meaning the meal is finished first. Coffee comes afterward.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Plain -고 can simply join actions; -고 나서 stresses the first is completed. Don't use it as if the actions happen together.

lessonExamples.englishHint: After eating, I drink coffee.
After doing my homework, I met a friend.

cards.englishHint: After drinking coffee, I go to work.
After exercising, I shower.
After washing my hands, I eat.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ 후에
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄴ 후에 to say 'after doing an action'. The action before 후에 is treated as completed.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the completed-action modifier: 먹다 → 먹은, 하다 → 한; then add 후에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 밥을 먹은 후에 약을 먹어요. — I take medicine after eating. 밥을 먹은 후에 약을 먹어요: after eating, the person takes medicine.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 수업 후에 is 'after class' with a noun. With a verb, don't attach 후에 directly to the bare stem: 먹후에 is wrong.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I take medicine after eating.
I went home after finishing work.

cards.englishHint: I went home after class ended.
After watching a movie, I drank coffee.
After reading a book, I go to sleep.

grammarPoints.title: -기 전에
grammarPoints.description: Use -기 전에 to say one action happens before another action. The first action is treated like an event you can refer to.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Remove 다 from the verb, add 기, then put 전에 after it: 자다 → 자기 전에. Continue with the earlier action.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 자기 전에 이를 닦아요. — I brush my teeth before sleeping. 자기 전에 이를 닦아요: 자다 ('sleep') becomes 자기, and 전에 means 'before'. Toothbrushing happens before sleep.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse 전에 after a noun (수업 전에) with verb + 기 전에 (먹기 전에).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I brush my teeth before sleeping.
I wash my hands before eating.

cards.englishHint: I close the door before going out.
I eat breakfast before going to school.
I drink water before exercising.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 때
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ 때 to say 'when' an action happens or a situation holds.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 을 때 after most consonant stems or ㄹ 때 after vowel stems: 가다 → 갈 때.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 집에 갈 때 버스를 타요. — When I go home, I take the bus. 집에 갈 때 버스를 타요: when going home, the speaker takes the bus.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This does not always mean a future event despite ㄹ. Context can make it habitual or present; keep 때 separate.

lessonExamples.englishHint: When I go home, I take the bus.
I read when I have time.

cards.englishHint: I rest when I am sick.

cards.fullSentence: 밥을 먹을 때 텔레비전을 안 봐요.
cards.englishHint: I do not watch TV while eating.
When it is cold, I drink warm tea.

grammarPoints.title: -고 있다
grammarPoints.description: Use -고 있다 for an action that is in progress: 'am reading', 'is studying'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take the action stem, attach 고, and add 있어요: 읽다 → 읽고 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 지금 책을 읽고 있어요. — I am reading a book now. 지금 책을 읽고 있어요: 읽다 becomes 읽고, followed by 있어요. The two-part form shows that reading is happening now.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't automatically use it for every English '-ing'. Some Korean verbs describe states, and their natural ongoing forms may differ.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I am reading a book now.
My friend is studying.

cards.englishHint: I'm listening to music right now.
Mom is cooking.
It is raining now.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 있다 (state after an action)
grammarPoints.hint: Use -아/어 있다 to describe a state that continues after an action finished, such as being seated, standing or a door remaining open.
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어 있다 to describe a state that continues after an action finished, such as being seated, standing or a door remaining open.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + -아/어 있다 (state after an action)

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For appropriate intransitive/result verbs, form 아/어 and follow it with 있다: 앉다 → 앉아 있어요, 서다 → 서 있어요, 열리다 → 열려 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 문이 열려 있어요. — The door is open. 문이 열려 있어요 means the door is now open as a result of an earlier opening; the sentence focuses on the present state.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not confuse this with -고 있다 for an action in progress. 앉고 있어요 is sitting down right now; 앉아 있어요 is already seated.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The door is open.
The child is sitting on a chair.

cards.englishHint: People are standing.
The cat is lying down.
The light is on.

grammarPoints.title: -는 중이다
grammarPoints.description: Use -는 중이다 to emphasize that someone is currently busy doing an action. It feels like 'in the middle of doing it'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the present action modifier -는, then add 중이에요: 공부하다 → 공부하는 중이에요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 지금 공부하는 중이에요. — I am in the middle of studying. 지금 공부하는 중이에요: 공부하다 becomes 공부하는, followed by 중이에요. Together they emphasize being in the middle of studying.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 중 is a separate noun-like word. Contrast -고 있어요 (ongoing action) with -는 중이에요 (busy in the middle of it).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I am in the middle of studying.
I am working right now.

cards.englishHint: I'm cleaning right now.
My friend is eating right now.
We are in a meeting now.

grammarPoints.title: -거나
grammarPoints.description: Use -거나 to present two possible ACTIONS or states: 'do A or do B'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 거나 to the first verb or descriptive-verb stem, then state the alternative: 읽다 → 읽거나.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 주말에는 책을 읽거나 영화를 봐요. — On weekends I read books or watch movies. 주말에는 책을 읽거나 영화를 봐요: on weekends, the speaker reads books or watches films.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For a choice between NOUNS, use (이)나. Don't put -거나 between simple nouns.

lessonExamples.englishHint: On weekends I read books or watch movies.
I rest at home or take a walk.

cards.englishHint: On weekends, I cook or rest.
For breakfast, I eat bread or rice.
In the evening, I exercise or listen to music.

grammarPoints.title: (이)나
grammarPoints.description: Use (이)나 to connect alternative NOUNS: 'coffee or tea'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이나; after a vowel, use 나: 책이나, 커피나.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 커피나 차를 마실래요? — Would you like coffee or tea? 커피나 차를 마실래요? asks if the listener would like coffee or tea.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Verb alternatives use -거나. (이)나 can also mean 'at least/around' in other contexts; this point teaches noun choice.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Would you like coffee or tea?
On weekends, I watch movies or dramas.

cards.englishHint: I read books or newspapers.
For lunch, I eat kimbap or ramen.
I take the bus or subway.

grammarPoints.title: -는 N
grammarPoints.description: Use -는 before a noun to describe someone or something by an ACTION happening now or habitually: 'the person who reads'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 는 to the action-verb stem, then put the noun right after it: 읽다 → 읽는 사람.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저기에서 책을 읽는 사람은 제 친구예요. — The person reading over there is my friend. 책을 읽는 사람: 읽는 describes 사람, the person doing the reading.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Descriptive verbs like 크다 normally use 큰, not 크는. Past action modifiers use -(으)ㄴ instead.

lessonExamples.fullSentence: 저기에서 책을 읽는 사람은 제 친구예요.
lessonExamples.englishHint: The person reading over there is my friend.
There are many students who study Korean.

cards.englishHint: The person smiling over there is our teacher.
People who exercise daily are healthy.
This is the café I often go to.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ N (action)
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄴ before a noun for an action that is already done: 'the clothes I bought'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For action verbs, add 은 after many consonant stems or ㄴ after vowel stems: 사다 → 산, 먹다 → 먹은.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 어제 산 옷이 예뻐요. — The clothes I bought yesterday are pretty. 어제 산 옷: 산 is 'bought', describing the clothes purchased yesterday.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This looks like the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ, but the meaning is different: for actions it points to completed action.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The clothes I bought yesterday are pretty.
The food I made is delicious.

cards.englishHint: The book I read yesterday was interesting.
The movie I watched yesterday was interesting.
I ate gimbap for breakfast.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ N
grammarPoints.hint: thing to do, future noun modifier
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ before a noun to describe something you will do or plan to do: 'a person I will meet'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 을 after many consonant stems, ㄹ after vowel stems, then the noun: 만나다 → 만날 사람.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 만날 사람은 제 친구예요. — The person I will meet tomorrow is my friend. 내일 만날 사람: 만날 describes the person the speaker will meet tomorrow.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This does not by itself finish a future-tense sentence. It modifies the noun that follows.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The person I will meet tomorrow is my friend.
What are we eating today?

cards.englishHint: I prepared the clothes I'll wear tomorrow.
I chose the movie I will watch this weekend.
I bought the book I will read tomorrow.

grammarPoints.title: -는 것
grammarPoints.description: Use -는 것 to refer to DOING an action as a thing or activity: 'reading books' or 'getting up early'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 는 to an action verb and put 것 after it; add an object/subject particle if the outer sentence needs one: 읽는 것을.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 책을 읽는 것을 좋아해요. — I like reading books. 저는 책을 읽는 것을 좋아해요: 'reading books' is the activity the speaker likes.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 것 is a separate word, and -는 것 differs from plain -기 in nuance and where each fits in a sentence.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I like reading books.
Getting up early is hard.

cards.englishHint: I like listening to music.
Exercising is good for your health.
I find cooking fun.

lessons.title: Trying Things and Talking About Experience

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 보다
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어 보다 to mean 'try doing something' or 'have tried it'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take the verb's 아/어 form and add 보다: 먹다 → 먹어 보다 → 먹어 보세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 이 음식을 먹어 보세요. — Please try this food. 이 음식을 먹어 보세요: 먹다 becomes 먹어; 보세요 politely invites the listener to TRY the food, not simply to look at it.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This auxiliary 보다 is not the verb 'to see' used literally. The spacing 먹어 보다 is a safe teaching default.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Please try this food.
I tried making Korean food.

cards.englishHint: I've tried kimchi.
Please try it on.
I tried wearing those clothes.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 to say you have done something at some time in your life.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the completed-action modifier and add 적이 있어요: 가다 → 간 적이 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 한국에 간 적이 있어요. — I have been to Korea. 한국에 간 적이 있어요 means 'I've been to Korea before' (there was a time I went).

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse past experience with a specific past event. 갔어요 states that you went; 간 적이 있어요 emphasizes having that experience.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I have been to Korea.
I have traveled alone before.

cards.englishHint: I've been to Busan before.
I have never eaten that food.
I have lived in Seoul before.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 본 적이 있다
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어 본 적이 있다 to say you have experienced TRYING an action before.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the 아/어 보다 auxiliary into its past modifier: 먹어 보다 → 먹어 본, then 적이 있어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 김치를 먹어 본 적이 있어요. — I have tried kimchi before. 김치를 먹어 본 적이 있어요: 먹다 → 먹어 보다 → 먹어 본. The phrase 적이 있어요 says the speaker has had that experience.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 본 refers to having tried an action; don't translate it as literally seeing something with your eyes.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I have tried kimchi before.
I have never tried wearing a hanbok.

cards.englishHint: I've tried driving on Jeju Island.

cards.fullSentence: 그 책을 읽어 본 적이 있어요.
cards.englishHint: I have read that book before.
I have visited Jeju Island before.

grammarPoints.title: -기로 하다
grammarPoints.description: Use -기로 하다 when you decide or agree to do something: 'decided to'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 기로 to the action stem, then 하다 in the right tense: 운동하다 → 운동하기로 했어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일부터 운동하기로 했어요. — I decided to exercise starting tomorrow. 내일부터 운동하기로 했어요 says the speaker made a decision to start exercising tomorrow.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is a decision, not just a possible plan. Compare 공부하려고 해요 (intend to study) with 공부하기로 했어요 (decided to study).

lessonExamples.englishHint: I decided to exercise starting tomorrow.
I decided to go with my friend.

cards.englishHint: I've decided to go to bed early this week.
I decided to rest at home today.
We decided to meet next week.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄹ 것 같다
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 to express a guess or prediction: 'I think it will...' or 'It seems likely...'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Make the -(으)ㄹ form of the verb first: 오다 → 올. Then add the separate words 것 같아요 to express a prediction.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 비가 올 것 같아요. — I think it will rain tomorrow. 내일 비가 올 것 같아요 is a prediction that rain will come tomorrow.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse this with -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 for a present descriptive state. The form before 것 changes with what you are judging.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think I will be busy this weekend.

cards.englishHint: I think it might snow tomorrow.
I think this food will be spicy.
I think my friend will arrive soon.

grammarPoints.title: -기 때문에
grammarPoints.description: Use -기 때문에 to state a reason: 'because of doing X' or 'because X happens'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 기 때문에 to a verb/adjective stem, then state the result: 오다 → 오기 때문에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 비가 오기 때문에 집에 있어요. — I am staying home because it is raining. 비가 오기 때문에 집에 있어요: rain is the reason the speaker stays home.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 때문에 often sounds more explanatory or formal than everyday -아/어서. Nouns typically use N 때문에 without -기.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I am staying home because it is raining.
I study because I have an exam.

cards.englishHint: I couldn't go because my stomach hurt.

cards.fullSentence: 너무 춥기 때문에 밖에 안 나가요.
cards.englishHint: I am not going outside because it is too cold.
I took a taxi because I had no time.

grammarPoints.title: -는데
grammarPoints.description: Use -는데 after an ACTION verb to give background, create contrast, or lead into what comes next.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For a present action verb, remove 다 and attach 는데: 오다 → 오는데. Then follow with the new information or contrast.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요. — It is raining, but I do not have an umbrella. 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요: it is raining, and the speaker provides the background for having no umbrella.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: -는데 is not always English 'but'. Sometimes it introduces a situation or gently sets up a request; descriptive verbs take another form.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It is raining, but I do not have an umbrella.
I am waiting for my friend, but they have not come yet.

cards.englishHint: It's raining outside, but I don't have an umbrella.

cards.fullSentence: 저는 커피를 마시는데 친구는 차를 마셔요.
cards.sentenceWithBlank: 저는 커피를 마시___ 친구는 차를 마셔요.
cards.englishHint: I drink coffee, but my friend drinks tea.
I am studying now, so I will call a little later.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)ㄴ데
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)ㄴ데 after most descriptive verbs (adjectives) to give background or set up a contrast.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 은데 after many consonant-ending descriptive stems and ㄴ데 after vowels: 춥다 → 추운데 (irregular).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 날씨가 추운데 밖에 갈까요? — It is cold, but shall we go outside? 날씨가 추운데 밖에 갈까요? gives 'it's cold' as background before suggesting going out.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Action verbs normally use -는데. Watch irregular descriptive stems such as 춥다 → 추운데 rather than a mechanical 춥은데.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It is cold, but shall we go outside?
This restaurant is expensive, but the food is good.

cards.englishHint: Those clothes are expensive but pretty.
The room is small but very clean.
I am busy today, but I have time tomorrow.

grammarPoints.title: -(이)ㄴ데
grammarPoints.description: Use -(이)ㄴ데 after a NOUN to say 'it's X, and/but...' while providing background or a contrast.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a consonant-ending noun, use 인데; after a vowel noun, use ㄴ데: 일요일 → 일요일인데.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘은 일요일인데 회사에 가요. — It is Sunday, but I am going to work. 오늘은 일요일인데 회사에 가요: although today is Sunday, someone is going to work.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This attaches to nouns, not verbs. Choose -는데 for action verbs and -(으)ㄴ데 for descriptive verbs.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It is Sunday, but I am going to work.
This is my friend, and they speak Korean well.

cards.fullSentence: 내일 시험인데 아직 공부 안 했어요.
cards.sentenceWithBlank: 내일 시험___ 아직 공부 안 했어요.
cards.englishHint: I have an exam tomorrow, but I haven't studied yet.
It is lunchtime; shall we eat together?
This is a library, and it is very quiet.

grammarPoints.title: -(으)면서
grammarPoints.description: Use -(으)면서 for actions happening at the same time: 'while doing A, do B'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 으면서 after most consonant stems or 면서 after vowel stems: 듣다 → 들으면서 (ㄷ irregular).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요. — I study while listening to music. 음악을 들으면서 공부해요: the speaker studies while listening to music.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Normally the two actions share a subject. If different people do the two actions, another structure may be more natural.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I study while listening to music.
I watch TV while eating.

cards.englishHint: I read while drinking coffee.
Please do not talk on the phone while walking.
I walk while talking with a friend.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어지다
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어지다 to describe a change in a quality: 'become colder', 'get easier'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take a descriptive stem and add 아/어지다: 춥다 → 추워지다 → 추워졌어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 날씨가 많이 추워졌어요. — The weather got much colder. 날씨가 많이 추워졌어요: 춥다 becomes 추워지다 ('grow cold'), then 추워졌어요 in the past. The weather changed into a colder state.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse change in a state (-아/어지다) with a change of circumstances leading someone to do something (-게 되다).

lessonExamples.englishHint: The weather got much colder.
Korean has become a little easier.

cards.englishHint: The weather has gotten cooler.
The weather got warmer.
The room became clean.

grammarPoints.title: -게
grammarPoints.description: -게 changes many descriptive verbs into a way of DOING an action: 'quietly', 'clearly', 'carefully'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 게 to the descriptive-verb stem, then put it before the action: 조용하다 → 조용하게.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 조용하게 말해 주세요. — Please speak quietly. 조용하게 말해 주세요: 조용하다 ('quiet') becomes 조용하게 ('quietly'). That word explains HOW the speaking should happen.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Not every English '-ly' translates mechanically to -게, and this -게 is different from the -게 in -게 되다.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Please speak quietly.
Please read accurately.

cards.englishHint: Please close the door quietly.
Please write in big letters.
Please play the music quietly.

grammarPoints.title: -게 되다
grammarPoints.description: Use -게 되다 when circumstances change and an action ends up happening or becoming the new situation.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 게 되다 to an action-verb stem: 살다 → 살게 되다 → 살게 됐어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 다음 달부터 서울에서 살게 됐어요. — I ended up moving to Seoul starting next month. 다음 달부터 서울에서 살게 됐어요: something happened or was decided so living in Seoul is now the outcome.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: It is not simply a neutral future-tense ending. It often emphasizes how the situation turned out, not only a free choice.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I ended up moving to Seoul starting next month.
I got a job at a new company.

cards.englishHint: I have ended up having to work overtime starting next week.

cards.fullSentence: 한국 친구를 만나서 한국어를 배우게 됐어요.
cards.englishHint: I started learning Korean after meeting a Korean friend.
I have come to get up early in the morning.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 두다
grammarPoints.description: Use -아/어 두다 when you do something now and leave the result ready for later.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Take the action's 아/어 form and add 두다: 열다 → 열어 두다 → 열어 두세요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 문을 열어 두세요. — Please leave the door open. 문을 열어 두세요: 열다 becomes 열어; 두세요 asks to keep the result in place. The door should remain open afterward.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This is different from merely opening a door once. The important idea is preserving the result.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Please leave the door open.
I prepared tomorrow's meal in advance.

cards.englishHint: I did my homework ahead of time.
I wrote down the phone number for later.
I bought water in advance.

grammarPoints.title: 보다
grammarPoints.description: 보다 after a noun means 'than', giving the comparison point.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 보다 after the item being compared AGAINST: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. — The subway is faster than the bus. 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요: the subway is fastER THAN the bus; 버스 is the comparison standard.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: The particle 보다 here is not the verb 보다 ('to see'). 더 can emphasize 'more', but is not required for the comparison.

lessonExamples.englishHint: The subway is faster than the bus.
Today is colder than yesterday.

cards.englishHint: It's warmer today than yesterday.
I prefer tea to coffee.
This bag is lighter than that one.

grammarPoints.title: 처럼
grammarPoints.description: 처럼 after a noun means 'like' or 'as', comparing manner or resemblance.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 처럼 right after the person or thing used as a model: 가수처럼.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 그 사람은 가수처럼 노래해요. — That person sings like a singer. 그 사람은 가수처럼 노래해요: 가수 means 'singer'. Adding 처럼 says the singing resembles that of a singer, without claiming the person is a singer.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 처럼 expresses resemblance, not a literal identity. For 'is a singer', use 가수예요.

lessonExamples.englishHint: That person sings like a singer.
She laughs like a child.

cards.englishHint: I speak slowly, like the teacher.
I want to speak Korean well like my friend.
I am busy today, just like yesterday.

grammarPoints.title: (으)로
grammarPoints.description: (으)로 can mean 'by/using', 'through', 'in the direction of', or 'as', depending on context.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Use 으로 after most consonant-ending nouns, 로 after vowel-ending nouns or nouns ending in ㄹ: 버스 → 버스로.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 버스로 학교에 가요. — I go to school by bus. 버스로 학교에 가요 means the bus is the means of travel. 연필로 써요 uses a pencil as a tool.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't pick 으로 after a final ㄹ: 서울로 is correct. Different meanings of (으)로 depend on the verb and situation.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I go to school by bus.
I write my name with a pencil.

cards.englishHint: I go to Seoul by train.
Please go to the right.
I take the subway to work.

grammarPoints.title: 마다
grammarPoints.description: 마다 means 'every' for a recurring time or individual item.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Choose the recurring time or group and attach 마다 directly: 아침마다, 주말마다, 사람마다. It means each occurrence or member.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 아침마다 운동해요. — I exercise every morning. 저는 아침마다 운동해요: 아침 is 'morning'. Adding 마다 makes the exercise a repeated habit, not just something done one morning.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 마다 implies repetition. It is different from 한 번 ('once') or 때마다 ('whenever') in more complex constructions.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I exercise every morning.
I meet friends every weekend.

cards.englishHint: Every class has homework.
This bus stops at every stop.
I study Korean every day.

grammarPoints.title: 밖에
grammarPoints.description: 밖에 with a negative verb means 'only' or 'nothing but', often conveying less than expected.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 밖에 to the limited noun/amount and follow with a NEGATIVE such as 없어요: 천 원밖에 없어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 지갑에 천 원밖에 없어요. — I only have 1,000 won in my wallet. 지갑에 천 원밖에 없어요: only 1,000 won is in the wallet; the following 없어요 is crucial.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Without negative wording, 밖에 is usually wrong for this 'only' meaning. 만 is a more neutral 'only' and does not require negation.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I only have 1,000 won in my wallet.
I only have ten minutes.

cards.englishHint: There is only water here.
I only drank water today.
I can only speak Korean.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어 버리다
grammarPoints.description: -아/어 버리다 means an action gets completely finished, often with feelings such as relief, regret, or surprise.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Form the verb's 아/어 shape first: 하다 → 해. Then add 버리다 and conjugate it: 해 버렸어요 (finished doing it).

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 숙제를 다 해 버렸어요. — I finished all my homework. 숙제를 다 해 버렸어요 means the homework got finished completely; it can carry relief.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: It does not always mean a bad outcome. The emotion depends on context: finishing an unpleasant task may feel good.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I finished all my homework.
I accidentally deleted the photo.

cards.englishHint: I ended up spending all the money.
I ate the entire cake.
I drank all the water.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어도
grammarPoints.description: -아/어도 means 'even if' or 'although', saying the next result still happens.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 아/어도 to the first clause and state the unchanged outcome: 오다 → 와도.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 비가 와도 가요. — I will go even if it rains. 비가 와도 가요: 오다 becomes 와도 ('even if it rains'). The main action 가요 still happens despite that condition.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not confuse concession -아/어도 with permission -아/어도 돼요. The following words determine the meaning.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I will go even if it rains.
I study even when I am tired.

cards.englishHint: I go outside even when it's cold.
I will buy it even if it is a little expensive.
It is okay even if you do not have time.

grammarPoints.title: 아무도 / 아무것도 + negative
grammarPoints.hint: Korean indefinite words such as 아무도 ('anyone/no one') and 아무것도 ('anything/nothing') usually pair with a negative predicate to mean 'nobody' or 'nothing'.
grammarPoints.description: Korean indefinite words such as 아무도 ('anyone/no one') and 아무것도 ('anything/nothing') usually pair with a negative predicate to mean 'nobody' or 'nothing'.
grammarPoints.structurePattern: [Verb / adjective / noun as indicated] + 아무도 / 아무것도 + negative

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Put 아무도 or 아무것도 where the person or thing belongs, then make the predicate negative: 아무도 없어요; 아무것도 안 먹어요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 아무도 안 왔어요. — Nobody came. 아무도 안 왔어요 means not a single person came because 아무도 is interpreted with the following negative form.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not leave the predicate affirmative for the intended negative meaning. Compare 누구나 and 아무나, which can mean 'anyone' in affirmative contexts.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Nobody came.
I didn't eat anything.

cards.englishHint: Nobody is coming today.
I couldn't see anything.
Nobody lives in this room.

grammarPoints.title: 그런데
grammarPoints.description: 그런데 connects sentences as 'but', 'by the way', or 'however', often shifting direction or topic.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Finish the first sentence, then start the next one with 그런데.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 오늘은 추워요. 그런데 코트가 없어요. — It is cold today, but I do not have a coat. 오늘은 추워요. 그런데 코트가 없어요: it's cold, but the speaker has no coat.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: 그런데 can also change topics gently. It's not a verb suffix; contrast하지만, which more directly marks opposition.

lessonExamples.englishHint: It is cold today, but I do not have a coat.

lessonExamples.fullSentence: 그 영화는 재미있어요. 그런데 너무 길어요.
lessonExamples.englishHint: That movie is interesting, but it is too long.

cards.fullSentence: 저는 커피를 좋아해요. 그런데 오늘은 차를 마셔요.
cards.sentenceWithBlank: 저는 커피를 좋아해요. ___ 오늘은 차를 마셔요.
cards.englishHint: I like coffee, but today I am drinking tea.
I study Korean, but it is still hard.

cards.fullSentence: 저는 서울에 살아요. 그런데 고향은 부산이에요.
cards.englishHint: I live in Seoul, but my hometown is Busan.

grammarPoints.title: -고 난 후에
grammarPoints.description: -고 난 후에 means 'after finishing an action', emphasizing that the action is already done.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 고 난 후에 to the first verb stem, then the next event: 운동하다 → 운동하고 난 후에.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 운동하고 난 후에 물을 마셔요. — I drink water after exercising. 운동하고 난 후에 물을 마셔요: drink water after working out is finished.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Do not treat it as a second unrelated 'after' word: compare -고 나서, which often expresses the same sequence more simply.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I drink water after exercising.
I rested after taking the exam.

cards.fullSentence: 영화를 보고 난 후에 집에 갔어요.
cards.englishHint: I went home after watching the movie.

cards.fullSentence: 밥을 먹고 난 후에 설거지를 해요.
cards.englishHint: I wash the dishes after eating.

cards.fullSentence: 일을 끝내고 난 후에 집에 갔어요.
cards.englishHint: I went home after finishing work.

grammarPoints.title: -아/어서 (sequence)
grammarPoints.description: -아/어서 can also link a first action to a next one: 'do A and then B'. Here it is SEQUENCE, not 'because'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Add 아서/어서 to the first verb stem; continue with a natural next action: 일어나다 → 일어나서.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 아침에 일어나서 세수해요. — I get up and then wash my face in the morning. 아침에 일어나서 세수해요: 일어나다 becomes 일어나서. Getting up comes first; washing up follows as a natural next action.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't confuse sequential -아/어서 with causal -아/어서; the full sentence's meaning determines whether you hear 'and then' or 'because'.

lessonExamples.englishHint: I get up and then wash my face in the morning.
I went home and rested.

cards.englishHint: I go inside and wash my hands.
I bought fruit at the market and came home.
I took the bus and went to school.

lessons.title: Optional Bridge: Reporting What People Say

grammarPoints.title: -ㄴ/는다고 하다
grammarPoints.description: Use -ㄴ/는다고 하다 to report what someone says about an ACTION: 'They say that...'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: For a present action verb, add ㄴ다고 after vowel stems or 는다고 after consonant stems, then 해요: 운동하다 → 운동한다고 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구가 매일 운동한다고 해요. — My friend says they exercise every day. 친구가 매일 운동한다고 해요 reports that the friend says they exercise daily.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Descriptive verbs usually use -다고, and nouns use -(이)라고; don't use the action-verb form for everything.

notes.title: Optional bridge
notes.content: Reported speech is often covered after core beginner grammar. This lesson is enrichment, not required for basic TOPIK I practice.

lessonExamples.englishHint: My friend says they exercise every day.
Minsu says he is reading a book now.

cards.englishHint: My friend says they are coming tomorrow.
My younger sibling said they were going to school.
My friend says they are eating dinner.

grammarPoints.title: -다고 하다 (adjective)
grammarPoints.description: Use -다고 하다 to report what someone says about a DESCRIPTION or state: 'They say it's busy'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Attach 다고 to a descriptive-verb stem and add 해요: 바쁘다 → 바쁘다고 해요.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 친구가 오늘 바쁘다고 해요. — My friend says they are busy today. 친구가 오늘 바쁘다고 해요: the friend reportedly says they are busy today.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: For action verbs use -ㄴ/는다고, and for nouns use -(이)라고. This lesson is a beyond-core-beginner bridge.

notes.title: Optional bridge
notes.content: Reported speech is often covered after core beginner grammar. This lesson is enrichment, not required for basic TOPIK I practice.

lessonExamples.englishHint: My friend says they are busy today.
Mom says the food is delicious.

cards.englishHint: Minsu says he is tired today.
My younger sibling said it was very cold.
The teacher says the exam is easy.

grammarPoints.title: (이)라고 하다
grammarPoints.hint: say it is called, say it is a noun
grammarPoints.description: Use -(이)라고 하다 to report a noun identity or give a name: 'I am called...' or 'They say it's...'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이라고; after a vowel, 라고: 민수 → 민수라고.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 저는 민수라고 해요. — My name is Minsu. 저는 민수라고 해요 is a common way to introduce one's name, literally 'I'm called Minsu'.

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: Don't use action-verb -ㄴ/는다고 after a noun. The noun's final consonant determines 이라고 vs 라고.

notes.title: Optional bridge
notes.content: Reported speech is often covered after core beginner grammar. This lesson is enrichment, not required for basic TOPIK I practice.

lessonExamples.englishHint: My name is Minsu.
They say that person is a teacher.

cards.englishHint: My name is Sujin.
This food is called kimchi.
My friend's name is Sujin.

grammarPoints.title: -다고요?
grammarPoints.description: -다고요? repeats or checks something heard, often with surprise: 'You said...?' or 'Really...?'.

notes.title: Build it step by step
notes.content: Repeat the reported content and end with 다고요? For actions, you may see ㄴ/는다고요?; for descriptions, 다고요?.

notes.title: Worked example
notes.content: 내일 비가 온다고요? — Did you say it will rain tomorrow? 내일 비가 온다고요? shows surprise or confirmation: 'You mean it's going to rain tomorrow?'

notes.title: Common trap
notes.content: This can sound challenging or sharp depending on tone. It is not the default friendly way to ask a neutral question.

notes.title: Optional bridge
notes.content: Reported speech is often covered after core beginner grammar. This lesson is enrichment, not required for basic TOPIK I practice.

lessonExamples.englishHint: Did you say it will rain tomorrow?
Did you say that restaurant is expensive?

cards.englishHint: Did you say there is no class tomorrow?
Did you say your friend is going today?
Did you say that movie is interesting?
